title: A general, rapid method for creating productive crops from wild plants

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a repeatable way to turn diverse, suitable wild plants into useful crops on a substantially shorter development path than conventional domestication. It would begin with plants that already possess valuable adaptations to their environments and combine the traits needed for cultivation: useful yield, harvestability, product quality, reliable reproduction and workable agricultural management. Retaining the original adaptation is part of the objective.

Conceptual synthesis: the central capability is predicting and producing a viable combination of traits across species. Editing a few known domestication genes can contribute to that process, but does not by itself demonstrate that the resulting plant can function as a crop. A general method would connect genetic changes to whole-plant performance, propagation, field management and the requirements of the intended food or oilseed product.

significance.text: Conditional significance: a reliable general method could broaden agriculture’s plant repertoire and let crop development begin with useful adaptations already present in wild species. Its revolutionary contribution would be to make the creation of new crops more predictable and repeatable, giving breeders more starting points for agricultural environments and uses that existing crops serve poorly.

Conditional downstream possibilities include more diverse crop portfolios and new food or oilseed options suited to particular growing conditions. These benefits depend on retaining the relevant adaptation while achieving acceptable productivity, quality and management requirements. Competitive yields, practical adoption and wider food-system benefits would require evidence for each resulting crop; expanding the number of cultivable species alone would not establish those outcomes.

Interpretive limit: rapid domestication should not be understood as making any wild plant into a valuable crop on demand. The intended generality concerns a method that transfers across diverse suitable species. Biological constraints and the requirements of different products and farming systems would still limit which plants are useful candidates.

missing_breakthrough.text: The proposed missing capability is reliable prediction and assembly of the full crop trait package across diverse wild plants while preserving useful adaptations. The supplied evidence does not establish how close research is to this capability or verify its present absence across the entire field. It nevertheless defines a coherent research objective beyond isolated domestication edits.

Engineering synthesis: a workable method would need to identify which traits limit cultivation in each species, determine genetic changes that improve them, and introduce and combine those changes without undermining other necessary functions. Yield, harvestability, quality, reproduction and management must work together. An improvement in one trait therefore needs evaluation in the resulting plant and production system, rather than being treated as sufficient evidence of successful domestication.

Engineering synthesis: transferability also requires a practical route from genetic intervention to fertile, stable planting material in each target species. The method must preserve the intended adaptation through trait combination and propagation, and establish that it remains useful under field conditions. These are proposed barriers implied by the objective; the supplied scientific artifact does not document their severity, solutions or failure rates across species.

current_state.text: The supplied research identifies a reported pennycress example: Barsanti Gautam, Brice A. Jarvis, Maliheh Esfahanian and colleagues, “Creating a new oilseed crop, pennycress, by combining key domestication traits using CRISPR genome editing,” attributed to Nature Plants on 22 January 2026, with DOI 10.1038/s41477-025-02202-7. The research describes combined domestication traits, improved oilseed characteristics and reduced weediness. These are reported findings from the supplied research, rather than findings verified from scientific text in the retained source.

According to the supplied review, the retained PubMed artifact contains only a cookie-access notice and provides no article identity, abstract, methods, results or publication details. The earlier description of an abstract-only assessment therefore overstates the scientific material available for verification. The claimed publisher-opening attempt is also not documented in the retained evidence. These access limitations leave the bibliographic details and reported traits unverified here; they do not show that the study or its findings are false.

Interpretive synthesis: if the reported pennycress findings are confirmed, they would illustrate combining crop-relevant traits in an individual species. They would not alone establish predictable crop creation across unrelated plant families, a general development-time advantage, stable seed systems or competitive field and food-system performance. The supplied material supports no verified quantitative estimates for those outcomes and does not establish the maturity of the pennycress result.

Coverage limitation: no bounded search record was supplied to assess developments through 1 November 2026. This record therefore cannot establish comprehensive current coverage or determine whether later work changes the assessment. The limitation concerns the available evidence and search history, rather than an inference that no further achievements exist.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independently create multiple useful food or oilseed crops from several unrelated wild plant families using a repeatable development method. Select sufficiently different starting plants to test transferability, and define the number and diversity of families before evaluation. Success across that set would establish demonstrated breadth within the tested scope, rather than literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Repeatably create multiple useful crops across unrelated wild plant families

completion_criteria.text: Proposed timing criterion: demonstrate a substantially shorter development path against explicit, relevant conventional domestication or crop-development comparisons. Define the starting point, endpoint and included stages in advance, including the work needed to obtain stable planting material and useful field performance. The supplied inputs provide no established numerical threshold for “rapid” or “substantially shorter.”
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrate substantially shorter development than relevant conventional crop-development pathways

completion_criteria.text: Proposed performance criterion: show stable reproduction and seed systems, useful yield, harvestability, product quality and workable management in replicated field and food-system trials. Compare performance with relevant alternatives for the intended use and environment, and demonstrate that the adaptation motivating selection of the wild species survives domestication and remains beneficial. Define “competitive” using explicit crop-specific measures rather than assuming a single yield benchmark fits every application.
completion_criteria.label: Replicated trials demonstrate stable, competitive crops retaining beneficial wild adaptations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and boundary criterion: have independent teams reproduce the method in additional target species, document development effort and failures, and identify conditions under which the method succeeds or fails. Evidence should distinguish producing an edited plant, producing a stable crop population and establishing a practically useful crop. These are proposed evaluation requirements, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Independent teams reproduce domestication in additional species, documenting effort and limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: AGR-01, cereal crops supplied predominantly by biological nitrogen fixation, and AGR-02, a transferable carbon-concentrating system for C3 staple crops, concern particular physiological capabilities. AGR-07 concerns creating viable crops from wild starting species. Either physiological capability could complement a new crop, but successful domestication would not establish either one.

Roster-based synthesis: AGR-03, reliable clonal seed reproduction across major hybrid crops, overlaps with the need for dependable reproduction and propagation. AGR-07 requires a stable seed system appropriate to the resulting crop, without requiring clonal seed reproduction. AGR-04, high-yield perennial versions of the major grain-crop portfolio, overlaps where a wild perennial provides a promising starting point; its target remains perennial versions of major grains, while AGR-07 addresses a broader crop-creation method.

Roster-based synthesis: AGR-05, productive staple farming with seawater and a closed salt balance, could intersect with domestication of plants selected for relevant environmental adaptations. Retaining a plant adaptation would not by itself demonstrate productive seawater farming or close a farming system’s salt balance. AGR-06, rapidly programmable, durable crop immunity, could improve a newly domesticated crop, but durable immunity and general crop creation remain separate capabilities.

Roster-based synthesis: AGR-08, economically accessible, end-to-end autonomous field farming, concerns farm operations. Crop architecture and harvestability developed under AGR-07 could affect compatibility with automated equipment, while neither innovation establishes the other. AGR-09, food crops that reliably build durable, additional soil carbon, could overlap with the selection of useful wild-plant traits; a new crop would still require separate evidence of durable, additional carbon storage.

change_log.change: Separated the conditional significance of broader agricultural choices from crop-specific productivity, adoption and food-system benefits.
change_log.reason: A general method would create opportunities, while each crop would still need to demonstrate practical value.

change_log.change: Developed proposed completion criteria around transferability, timing comparisons, stable seed systems, replicated performance, retained adaptation and independent reproduction.
change_log.reason: The original terms “several unrelated families,” “substantially shorter” and “competitive” require operational definitions and must not be presented as established standards.

unresolved_issues: Scientific text is needed to verify the pennycress article’s identity, publication details, combined traits, seed composition, reduced weediness and demonstrated experimental scope.
The supplied evidence does not establish the present breadth or limitations of de novo domestication across species, or whether another result already meets part of the proposed capability.
No bounded search record establishes coverage through 1 November 2026.
The proposed evaluation still needs explicit species and family selection, timing endpoints, comparison baselines, performance thresholds, trial scope and seed-system stability requirements.
Retention of useful adaptations while combining the complete crop trait package remains an objective whose feasibility and reliability cannot be assessed from the retained artifact.

brief.title: Rapid creation of useful crops from wild plants
possible: Farmers could grow new food and oil crops developed from wild plants already suited to their growing conditions. Breeders could use a repeatable, much faster route to combine useful harvests, reliable reproduction and manageable plants while keeping the wild traits that made them worth choosing.
why: Agriculture could draw on a wider range of plants. Breeders would have more starting points for growing conditions and uses that existing crops serve poorly, giving farmers and food producers more options.

sources.showed: Targeted DNA changes produced high-yielding pennycress with less seed fibre and lower levels of erucic acid and glucosinolate, compounds targeted to improve seed quality. Other changes reduced its tendency to return as a weed.
sources.quote: High-yielding varieties were created with seed compositions such as 'double-low' canola (low erucic acid and reduced glucosinolate) and reduced seed fibre content.
sources.cited_for: The study supports combining several traits needed to turn a wild plant into a crop.
sources.not_established: Success in pennycress does not establish a predictable method across unrelated plants or a shorter development path.

sources.showed: Targeted DNA changes altered wild tomato growth, fruit size, fruit number and nutritional value. Some initial changes failed, and the researchers revised their targets.
sources.quote:
Compared with the wild parent, 
our engineered lines have a threefold increase in fruit size 
and a tenfold increase in fruit number.
sources.cited_for: The study supports improving several crop traits together in a wild tomato.
sources.not_established: Improved tomato traits do not establish competitive field performance or transferability across unrelated plant families.

sources.showed: The researchers used knowledge of tomato genes to improve groundcherry, a little-developed crop. DNA changes altered plant shape, increased fruit concentration along shoots and enlarged fruit.
sources.quote:
Notably, these plants were 
more compact than the wild type, and we validated this phenotype in 
homozygous and biallelic null Ppr-spCR T1 progeny plants (Fig. 2b,c).
sources.cited_for: The study supports transferring knowledge of crop traits between related plants.
sources.not_established: Trait improvements in a crop related to tomato do not establish a general route from wild plants to practically useful crops.

shown: Gautam and colleagues combined crop-relevant traits in pennycress. Zsögön and colleagues improved wild tomato, while Lemmon and colleagues improved groundcherry. Together, these studies demonstrate useful changes in particular plants; they do not establish predictable crop creation across diverse wild species.
missing: A repeatable method still needs to combine yield, harvestability, quality, reproduction and manageable growth across diverse suitable wild plants.
New crops still need to retain their useful wild adaptations through reproduction and under field conditions.
Development speed and practical crop performance still need testing against relevant conventional pathways and agricultural alternatives.

milestones.label: Useful crops repeatedly created across unrelated plant families
milestones.explanation: A repeatable method would have to produce useful food or oil crops from a predefined range of unrelated wild plant families. This would establish how broadly it works.

milestones.label: Substantially faster development than relevant conventional routes
milestones.explanation: Comparisons would have to show substantially shorter development, including stable planting material and useful field performance. This would establish the speed advantage.

milestones.label: Competitive crops retain useful wild adaptations in repeated trials
milestones.explanation: Repeated field and food-system trials would have to show reliable seed supply, useful harvests, quality and manageable crops that retain beneficial wild traits. This would establish practical value.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce success and document limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to create additional useful crops and document effort, failures and conditions for success. This would distinguish a reproducible method from isolated successes.

uncertain: Can breeders reliably combine all the necessary crop traits without losing the wild adaptation they wanted?
Which species and plant families provide a sufficiently demanding test of the method’s breadth?
What development endpoints, speed advantage and crop-specific performance thresholds should count as success?

page.title: De novo crop domestication across plant families
page.definition: A repeatable method converts wild plants from different botanical families into crops that retain a chosen wild adaptation while combining harvestable yield, product quality and stable reproduction. Development takes less elapsed time than conventional domestication measured to the same cultivar-release endpoint.

goal.need: Crop production is concentrated within the much larger set of plants historically cultivated for food, as quantified below. NovoCrops seeks to broaden crop choice by domesticating plants whose existing stress adaptations are difficult to transfer into established varieties.

figures.caption: Crop diversity reported in FAO’s 2019 assessment
rows: Major contributions to food production globally, regionally or nationally
Account for 66% of total crop production
figures.note: The production share concerns crop production, rather than dietary calories.

statements.body: FAO Commission on Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture
statements.quote: Biodiversity makes production systems and livelihoods more resilient to shocks and stresses, including those caused by climate change.

statements.body: NovoCrops, University of Copenhagen and Aarhus University
statements.quote: Using targeted genome editing techniques, including non-GMO approaches, we will de novo domesticate six future crops
statements.context: The programme includes wild barley and potato relatives, alfalfa, lupin, quinoa and intermediate wheatgrass.

completion.title: One domestication pipeline produces registered crops from wild plants in two plant families.
completion.criterion: The same pipeline, repeated in wild species from at least two botanical families, produces registered food or oilseed cultivars. Each meets requirements for harvestable yield, product quality, reproduction and management set beforehand by its crop-development programme, retains the wild adaptation used to select its progenitor, and passes replicated field evaluation. Each reaches registration in less elapsed time than a conventional domestication comparator measured from equivalent starting material to the same endpoint. Independent teams reproduce the pipeline and its time advantage.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; proposed criterion without an externally adopted cross-family benchmark.
completion.basis: Searches of FAO/USDA material, NovoCrops targets and published domestication roadmaps found no cross-family completion benchmark or agreed development-time advantage. Registration supplies the Yu–Li roadmap’s endpoint. Two families is the minimum test beyond one family. Crop-specific requirements follow DeHaan’s call for a “custom set of domestication milestones”. This is an Atlas proposal.

milestones.title: A target plant yields regenerated plants carrying targeted genome edits.
milestones.criterion: A regenerated plant carries sequence-confirmed edits at a chosen locus. T0 denotes the first regenerated generation. Groundcherry, published 1 October 2018: Ppr-AGO7-edited T0 plants. Wild tomato, published 1 October 2018: 10 primary T0 lines, three grown to maturity. Pennycress, published 22 January 2026: CRISPR-Cas9 mutants combined in breeding lines; the accessible preview gives no transformation sample size.
milestones.set_by: Plant genome-editing community; edited T0 plants are an experimental demonstration used by Lemmon et al. for groundcherry and Zsögön et al. for wild tomato, both in 2018.
milestones.threshold_quote: First-generation (T0) plants were chimeric for Ppr-AGO7 mutations

milestones.title: Edited plants transmit an improved domestication trait to seed-grown progeny.
milestones.criterion: A targeted edit and its cultivation phenotype recur in seed-grown progeny. The cited studies use T1 or later progeny, without a universal generation count. Groundcherry, published 1 October 2018: compact T1 mutants; at least six independent replicates per Figure 2 experiment. Wild tomato, published 1 October 2018: traits persisted in T2/T3; four loci were edited in all 50 tested T1 offspring of one primary line. Pennycress, published 22 January 2026: stacked seed-quality mutations; the accessible preview does not establish a progeny-generation test.
milestones.set_by: Plant genome-editing community; confirmation of mutant phenotypes in seed progeny is used by Lemmon et al. for groundcherry and Zsögön et al. for wild tomato. Their generation numbers are experimental conditions, not universal thresholds.
milestones.threshold_quote: we validated this phenotype in homozygous and biallelic null Ppr-spCR T1 progeny plants

milestones.title: Bred, edited plants produce a measured seed or fruit harvest in field trials.
milestones.criterion: Bred, edited plants produce a field harvest evaluated for agronomic performance. The roadmap specifies field evaluation without a universal minimum yield or trial size. Pennycress, published 22 January 2026: seed yield was tested in 5 ft × 10 ft plots, with three replicate plots per line except wild type, which had four. Most lines grew comparably to controls; hag1 hag3 double mutants were an exception. The cited wild-tomato and groundcherry papers do not establish this field stage.
milestones.set_by: De novo domestication roadmap described as generally agreed by Yu and Li in 2022, step 3. The published stage requires breeding and field evaluation but supplies no numerical performance pass mark.
milestones.threshold_quote: editing of domestication-related genes followed by breeding and field evaluation

milestones.title: A cultivar produced by de novo domestication obtains cultivar registration.
milestones.criterion: A cultivar derived from an edited wild or weakly domesticated plant completes the applicable cultivar-registration process, step 4 of the published roadmap. The jurisdiction’s actual requirements apply; the roadmap supplies no universal numerical registration threshold. Registration status remains unverified for the experimental wild-tomato, groundcherry and pennycress lines tracked here.
milestones.set_by: De novo domestication roadmap described as generally agreed by Yu and Li in 2022, step 4. This identifies an endpoint for an individual cultivar, rather than a test of a method’s transfer between plant families.

not_found: No externally published cross-family completion benchmark or agreed development-time advantage was found in searches of programme targets and domestication roadmaps.
No cultivar-registration record linked to the experimental lines in the three tracked plants was identified.
The publisher’s full pennycress article could not be opened; its publisher-supplied preview and figure legends were accessible on ResearchGate.

results.finding: Pennycress CRISPR-Cas9 mutations were identified and stacked; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The text does not establish plant regeneration or sequence confirmation of an edit.
results.quote: As a remedy, we performed de novo domestication of the freeze-tolerant, rapid-cycling wild brassica Thlaspi arvense L. (field pennycress), identifying and stacking CRISPR-Cas9-induced mutations that have minimal impacts on seed yields.

results.finding: Pennycress seed glucosinolate content fell 75% with combined mutations; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The text does not establish recurrence of the edits and phenotype in seed-grown progeny.
results.quote: Seed glucosinolate content was reduced by 75% by combining mutations in R2R3-MYB (MYB28/HAG1) and basic helix-loop-helix MYC (MYC3) transcription factors.

results.finding: Stacked pennycress mutations had minimal impacts on seed yields; sample size and yield values not stated.
results.detail: The text reports a yield result but does not establish that it came from a field harvest.
results.quote: As a remedy, we performed de novo domestication of the freeze-tolerant, rapid-cycling wild brassica Thlaspi arvense L. (field pennycress), identifying and stacking CRISPR-Cas9-induced mutations that have minimal impacts on seed yields.

results.finding: Two wild-tomato T0 plants had sequence-confirmed mutations at all four targeted loci.
results.detail: These were among three successfully transformed T0 lines in the second editing experiment.
results.quote:
Sequencing of T 0 plants 5 and 8 identi -
fied loss-of-function mutations in all four targeted loci in both lines
(Supplementary Fig. 5 and Supplementary Dataset 2).

results.finding: Two T2 wild-tomato lines showed compact, determinate growth associated with inherited SP edits.
results.detail: The T1 parents of both lines carried homozygous SP deletions. Height and sympodial index were measured using six plants per group.
results.quote:
Similarly, 
loss of SP function in S. pimpinellifolium resulted in compact plants with 
reduced height, reduced number of sympodial units and determinate 
growth when compared with WT S. pimpinellifolium (Fig. 1b–g).

results.finding: Groundcherry: multiple T0 plants carried sequenced Ppr-SP edits; 2 guide RNAs were used.
results.detail: The number of edited T0 plants is not stated.
results.quote: b, CRISPR–Cas9 targeting of SP in P. pruinosa. Ppr-spCR mutant alleles identified by PCR and sequencing in T 0 transgenic plants are shown.

results.finding: Groundcherry Ppr-SP-edited T1 plants showed compact growth across 6 independent experiments.
results.detail: The compact phenotype was validated in homozygous and biallelic null progeny; the severe null phenotype may limit fruit production.
results.quote:
In c , e and g, representative images of Ppr-sp CR homozygous T 1 plants from six repeated independent experiments 
with similar results are shown.

results.finding: Pennycress: 20 T2 progeny were tested; targeted ROD1 mutations and altered seed oil profiles were inherited.
results.detail: Three T1 parent plants carried distinct ROD1 edits. Mutations segregated as recessive, and seeds from homozygous mutant plants had higher oleic acid content than wild type under controlled conditions.
results.quote: The lipid profile changes were also consistent between siblings and from generation to generation, suggesting low plasticity to these traits, at least under our controlled growth chamber conditions.

results.finding: Improved pennycress tt8-t/ARV1, in three replicate plots per site, had 20%–40% lower seed yield with pelleting than untreated plants.
results.detail: The field trial measured seed yield, but the text does not establish that either improved line was gene-edited. Two sites could not be harvested because of weed competition.
results.quote: Seed yield for tt8-t/ARV1 did not increase over the untreated with any treatment and was reduced by 20%–40% when pelleted.

results.finding: Wild tomato S. peruvianum: 11 of 24 regenerated SpProSys plants showed targeted mutagenesis.
results.quote: Upon sequencing of the 24 regenerated  SpProSys  plants, 11 showed target mutagenesis (45.8%,  Table 1 ).

results.finding: Wild tomato: 2 of 6 SpSGS3 #7 T1 progeny carried only mutant alleles and showed a wiry phenotype.
results.detail: The edit and a visible mutant phenotype recur in seed-grown progeny, but the phenotype is wiry/sterile (and mutants show higher TYLCV), not an improved domestication trait.
results.quote: Among the six progeny of  SpSGS3 #7, two progeny harbored the mutated alleles only ( Supplemental Figure S5 ); these plants also showed a wiry phenotype ( spsgs3 #7-2;  Supplemental Figure S9b ).

results.finding: Pennycress: 26 T4 progeny yielded homozygous FAE1 A-insertion, T-deletion and 4-bp-deletion lines; edits sequence-confirmed.
results.detail: Sequence-confirmed fae1 edits are reported in T4 homozygous lines; the text does not show sequence-confirmed edits in the first regenerated generation (T0).
results.quote: By sequencing 26 T 4  progeny arising from those T 3  plants, we identified a plant homozygous for a single A insertion and a plant homozygous for a single T deletion in  FAE1  along with plants homozygous for the 4 bp deletion

results.finding: Pennycress: three homozygous fae1 lines (4-bp deletion, A insertion, T deletion) had negligible seed-oil erucic acid in progeny.
results.detail: Homozygous fae1 lines were recovered after sequencing 26 T4 progeny, and their seed oil had negligible erucic/eicosenoic acid, showing edit plus domestication phenotype in seed-grown progeny.
results.quote: Seeds from homozygous  fae1‐3 , fae1‐4 and fae1‐5 plants were analysed for TAG fatty acid composition, revealing negligible amounts of erucic (C22:1) and eicosenoic (C20:1) acids in all three lines

results.finding: HPPD G419A homozygous HDR line recovered from ≈800 T2 seedlings; Sanger-confirmed edit.
results.detail: ALS P187S HDR screening also recovered 3 survivors from ≈20,000 T2 seeds; both HDR events were Sanger-validated.
results.quote: In the HPPD HDR lines, PACE genotyping of T 2  seeds yielded a homozygous HPPD G419A  line among approximately 800 seedlings analyzed

results.finding: T3 ALS P187S HDR lines maintained VOLTA tolerance at 2×; n not stated; edit/phenotype recur in seed-grown progeny.
results.quote: Homozygous  als‐b  HDR lines maintained robust VOLTA tolerance at 2× concentration during rosette‐stage overtop application (Figure  6A ).

results.finding: T3 ALS P187S HDR lines (n not stated) had seed yield measured under 1× VOLTA; no significant penalty (p=0.5845); not reported as field.
results.detail: Seed yield was measured for HDR-derived T3 lines; the text places these growth/yield assays in greenhouse/controlled conditions, not a field trial, so the field-harvest criterion is only partially addressed.
results.quote: Further, when grown to maturity, yield analysis revealed no statistically significant seed yield penalty ( p ‐value = 0.5845) in 1× VOLTA sprayed  als‐b  plants compared with non‐sprayed  als‐b  controls (Figure  6B ).
